evidence_quotes.quote: This study aimed to estimate the proportion of people with access to latrine facilities and the proportion of people who practice open defecation in the villages of Perambalur, Tamil Nadu.
For this study, we selected 329 households using a convenient sampling method from two villages in the Perambalur area.
An independent t-test found no statistically significant relationship between the availability of household latrines and the number of girls or boys, age, or family income.

However, only 24% of the survey participants who had bathrooms had benefited from government initiatives. The eligibility requirements specified in the funding system may be to blame for this. However, further research is required for this discussion.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household sanitation service access in rural villages, specifically availability of household latrines, shared toilets, underground drainage/sewage disposal, and open-air defecation.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, no rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism governing access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, or enforcement) is empirically measured or analysed; the authors explicitly note in the Discussion that eligibility requirements in the funding system might explain why only 24% benefited from government initiatives, but state that further research is required to study that question. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study's analytical exposures are purely socio-demographic and housing characteristics (family size, age/gender composition, income, religion, and kutcha/semi-pucca/pucca house type) alongside behavioral/cost perceptions, with only univariate descriptive counts of whether households benefited from (24%) or were unaware of (22% of non-toilet homes) a generic government toilet-construction scheme and health education sources.
criterion_notes.c3: Primary quantitative empirical study conducting semi-structured questionnaire interviews across 329 rural households analysed using descriptive statistics, independent t-tests, and chi-square/Fisher's exact tests.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household sanitation access outcomes: household latrine availability (64.1%), open-air defecation practice (52.3%), and underground sewage disposal access (4.7% of toilet-owning households).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (329 households in two rural villages, Senjeri and Siruvachur, in Perambalur district), analytical exposures (demographic, income, religion, and house-type variables), outcomes (household latrine availability and open defecation), and study design (community-based cross-sectional analytical study) are clearly reported.

population_and_sample: 329 rural households (one respondent per household, preferably head of family) in two villages (Senjeri and Siruvachur) in Perambalur district, Tamil Nadu
exposure: Socio-demographic and housing characteristics (household age/gender composition, family size, monthly family income, religion, and house type: kutcha, semi-pucca, pucca); descriptive self-reported reasons for lacking a toilet and receipt/awareness of government toilet-building scheme
outcome: Household latrine availability (own or shared toilet vs. no toilet facility), open-air defecation practice, and access to underground sewage disposal
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Note on metadata: the retrieved PDF matches the record's exact Title, Year (2022), and DOI (10.7759/cureus.32547), confirming it is the target article (the bibliographic record's author field appears to carry an upstream indexing error, whereas the PDF lists Tamilarasan M et al.). Substantively, this cross-sectional survey of 329 rural households in Tamil Nadu examines household latrine availability and open-air defecation (satisfying c1, c3, c4), but its analytical exposures are purely socio-demographic and housing-material variables (age, gender composition, family size, monthly income, religion, and kutcha/semi-pucca/pucca house structure) along with descriptive behavioral/cost barriers and univariate counts of government toilet-scheme uptake. It does not examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, or rule-type governance mechanism governing sanitation access; potential funding eligibility requirements are only mentioned speculatively in one sentence as a topic for future research.
